Nightfall means the time when night begins — the moment, or the brief period, when daylight finally fades and darkness takes over the sky.

Think of a full day: the sun rises in the morning, shines through the day, then slowly sinks toward the horizon in the evening. After the sun dips below the horizon, there is still a little bit of soft, fading light in the sky for a while (this is called dusk or twilight — a dim, in-between light). Nightfall is the point when even that last bit of lingering light disappears and true darkness arrives. The day is fully over. Night has officially begun.

So if you picture the sky going from bright blue → golden → orange and pink → deep purple → black, nightfall is roughly that final shift to black.
How it is different from similar words

Since "nightfall" sits close to several other words, knowing the differences will sharpen your understanding:

  • Sunset is the specific moment the sun goes below the horizon. It's earlier than nightfall — the sky is still lit up with colours.
  • Dusk / Twilight is the soft, dim period after sunset but before full darkness. The sky still has some glow.
  • Nightfall is when that glow is gone. Darkness is complete. Night has arrived.
  • Evening is a broader, more casual word for the later part of the day, roughly from about 6 PM onward. It includes all of dusk and nightfall within it.
  • Night refers to the whole dark period until sunrise. Nightfall is merely the beginning of night — the threshold you cross to enter it.

A simple way to feel the order: Sunset → Dusk/Twilight → Nightfall → Night.

Nightfall has a slightly literary and poetic quality to it. It is a real, everyday word — not fancy or old-fashioned — but it carries a sense of weight and atmosphere that a plain word like "dark" or "night" does not. When a writer or speaker chooses "nightfall," they are usually trying to paint a picture or set a mood: the quiet closing of the day, perhaps a sense of urgency, mystery, beauty, or even danger as light gives way to darkness.

You will find it very often in literature, poetry, songs, films, and storytelling. But it also appears naturally in ordinary speech, especially in phrases like "before nightfall" or "by nightfall."

Nightfall is an uncountable noun, which means you do not say "a nightfall" or "two nightfalls" in normal use. It is most commonly used without any article (no "a" or "the") in prepositional phrases that express time.

The most common patterns are:

  • Before nightfall — meaning before it gets dark
  • By nightfall — meaning by the time it gets dark
  • At nightfall — meaning at the moment/time when darkness arrives
  • After nightfall — meaning once darkness has come
  • Until nightfall — meaning up to the point when darkness arrives

These phrases work just like similar time expressions: "before noon," "by midnight," "at dawn."

1. "We need to reach the village before nightfall."
(They must arrive while there is still light — darkness is approaching.)

2. "The workers finished building the shelter by nightfall."
(They completed it just as night was arriving.)

3. "At nightfall, the city's streetlights flickered on one by one."
(The moment night began, the lights came on.)

4. "It is not safe to travel alone on that road after nightfall."
(Once it is dark, the road becomes dangerous.)

5. "She sat by the window and watched nightfall settle over the mountains."
(She watched as darkness slowly came over the mountains — nightfall as a process.)

6. "The soldiers were ordered to retreat before nightfall."
(A deadline set by the approaching darkness.)

7. "Rain began to fall as nightfall approached."
(As darkness was drawing near.)

Notice that in all these sentences, nightfall acts as a time marker — it signals when something happens, much like "dawn," "noon," or "midnight" do. It answers the question "When?" It is a moment in the daily cycle of light and dark, and a particularly evocative one, because it marks the end of the visible day and the beginning of the mysterious, quiet hours of night.
